questions.stem: The Harappan civilisation was discovered in 1921. Who led the initial excavation at Harappa?
questions.explanation: Harappa (Punjab, now Pakistan) was excavated in 1921 by Daya Ram Sahni (under ASI). Mohenjo-daro (Sindh, now Pakistan) was excavated in 1922 by R. D. Banerji. Sir JOHN MARSHALL (ASI Director General) announced the discovery of this civilisation in 1924 through a landmark article in The Illustrated London News, giving it the name 'Indus Valley Civilisation'. Mortimer Wheeler excavated in the 1940s, refining chronology. Now called Harappan or Indus-Sarasvati Civilisation. Flourished 2600-1900 BCE (Mature phase). Spread over ~1.25 million sq km — across modern Pakistan, NW India, and eastern Afghanistan.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Lothal, famous for what specific feature, is an Indus Valley site located in which state?
questions.explanation: LOTHAL (Bhal region of Gujarat, near Gulf of Khambhat) is FAMOUS for the world's oldest known dockyard (c. 2400 BCE) — confirming Harappan maritime trade with Mesopotamia. Also notable: fire altars (7), a bead-making factory, a chess-like board game. Excavated by S. R. Rao (1954-63). Tidal dockyard of 214 × 36 m with sluice gates. Contrast site features: Great Bath = Mohenjo-daro (Sindh, Pakistan); Fire altars = Kalibangan (Rajasthan) AND Lothal; Ploughed field = Kalibangan (oldest-known ploughed field, earthquake evidence); Largest site = Rakhigarhi (Haryana, ~350 ha); Harbour/coastal = Lothal, Dholavira, Surkotada.

questions.stem: Which Indus Valley site yielded the famous 'Dancing Girl' bronze statue?
questions.explanation: The 'DANCING GIRL' (10.5 cm tall, bronze, lost-wax casting technique) was excavated from Mohenjo-daro in 1926 by Ernest Mackay. Dated ~2500 BCE. Shows a nude young female with bangles on her left arm, hand on hip in a dance posture. Currently in the National Museum, New Delhi. Other famous Mohenjo-daro artefacts: 'Priest-King' bust (now in Karachi National Museum, Pakistan — disputed artefact), the Great Bath, the Great Granary. Harappa yielded: the 'Red Jasper Male Torso' (the 'Harappan Dancing Figure' or the Red-stone male figure, 10 cm).

questions.stem: Rakhigarhi, now considered the LARGEST Harappan site, is in which state?
questions.explanation: Rakhigarhi (Hisar district, Haryana) is now recognised as the LARGEST Harappan site (~350 ha — surpassing Mohenjo-daro's ~250 ha; sometimes called 'Rakhi-Shahpur' after the twin villages). Excavations by Vasant Shinde (Deccan College) and ASI have uncovered planned streets, drains, burials, seals, a jewellery workshop, and most famously — ANCIENT DNA from a 4500-year-old female skeleton (2018-19 study by Shinde & Niraj Rai), showing Harappan people had NO Steppe/Aryan ancestry — supporting the 'Aryan migration post-Harappa' theory. Previous 'largest site' status shifted: Mohenjo-daro > Harappa > Ganweriwala (Pakistan) > Dholavira > Rakhigarhi.

questions.stem: Kalibangan, known for its pre-Harappan ploughed field and fire altars, is located in which state?
questions.explanation: Kalibangan ('black bangles' in Punjabi — named after black terracotta bangles found in abundance) is located on the left bank of the Ghaggar river in Hanumangarh district, Rajasthan. Excavated by B. B. Lal and B. K. Thapar (1961-69). Unique for: (1) the world's EARLIEST EVIDENCE of a ploughed field (pre-Harappan, c. 2800 BCE — crisscross furrow pattern suggesting two crops grown simultaneously); (2) SEVEN FIRE ALTARS (suggesting fire-worship, a rare religious clue); (3) evidence of the OLDEST recorded EARTHQUAKE (c. 2600 BCE, may have caused abandonment); (4) lower town also fortified (unusual). Kalibangan sits on the now-dry Saraswati river.

questions.stem: Surkotada, a Harappan site in Gujarat, provided the ONLY conclusive evidence from Indus sites of the presence of:
questions.explanation: Surkotada (Kutch, Gujarat), excavated by J. P. Joshi (1964-68), yielded the ONLY confirmed Harappan-era HORSE bones (dated c. 2000 BCE) — a significant finding because the absence of horses in Harappan art/bones was long cited as evidence that the Harappan people were NOT Aryan/Indo-European. The horse remains at Surkotada were verified by archaeo-zoologist Sándor Bökönyi (Hungarian expert). Horses are prominent in Vedic Aryan culture, which developed AFTER the Harappan civilisation declined. Iron came much later (c. 1200 BCE PGW culture). Harappans used pictographic seals, not Brahmi. Coinage dates only to ~6th c. BCE (Mahajanapadas).

questions.stem: The Harappan civilisation is best known for its town planning. Which of the following is NOT characteristic of a typical Indus city layout?

options.option_text: Grid pattern streets intersecting at right angles
Advanced underground drainage with soak pits

questions.explanation: The HARAPPANS are notable for having NO monumental temples or palaces — unlike contemporary Mesopotamia and Egypt. This puzzles archaeologists: was it an egalitarian society, or was their religion domestic? Characteristic features: (a) GRID-pattern streets; (b) Citadel + Lower Town division (upper western citadel for public/administrative buildings, lower eastern for residences); (c) Standardised burnt bricks (ratio 1:2:4 — length:breadth:height); (d) ADVANCED drainage — covered drains, soak pits, manholes; (e) Granaries; (f) Uniform weights and measures; (g) Seals with pictographic script (~400 characters, undeciphered); (h) No large stone sculptures. Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro is the closest to a 'public' structure but not a temple.

questions.stem: Dholavira, a 2021 UNESCO WHS, uniquely had which advanced engineering feature?

options.option_text: Sophisticated water conservation system with 16 reservoirs

questions.explanation: DHOLAVIRA (Khadir Bet, Rann of Kutch, Gujarat) is famed for its INGENIOUS WATER HARVESTING system — 16 stone-lined reservoirs comprising ~10% of the city area, collecting monsoon runoff and water from two seasonal streams (Mansar and Manhar). Also known for: (1) tripartite city plan (Citadel + Middle Town + Lower Town — unique among Indus sites); (2) the DHOLAVIRA SIGNBOARD — a 10-sign inscription above a gateway, possibly the oldest 'signboard' in history; (3) rock-cut architecture; (4) declining phase shows gradual settlement of a much-reduced population. Inscribed as India's 40th UNESCO WHS on 27 July 2021.
